title: MB9-11084
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of the Arab Republic of Egypt, is appealing the April 25, 2019, decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of the Arab Republic of Egypt, is appealing the April 25, 2019, decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

The appellant submitted the following written account, which is found in the Basis of Claim Form1 (BOC Form). The appellant states that he fears being imprisoned and tortured if he returns to Egypt. He states that in XXXX 2013, after his brother left the country because he was a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, the military secret service began investigating his brother and monitoring the movements of his family members. The appellant points out that he did not see a future for himself under the regime in place and therefore he left Egypt on XXXX XXXX, 2016, to continue his education in Canada. He indicates that, in Canada, he hosted an Egyptian who turned out to be an activist working against President Sissi's regime and the military, and that warrants for his arrest had been issued. He then indicates that he learned that military officers went to see his parents twice, once in XXXX 2017 and again in XXXX 2018. They asked about his activities in Canada against the regime in place and warned his parents that an arrest warrant could be issued for him. After this last incident, the appellant decided to claim refugee protection in April 2018.
The RPD rejected the appellant's claim for refugee protection for lack of credibility.

On appeal, the appellant submitted the following arguments: 1-The Egyptian authorities never told the appellant's father that he was accused of belonging to the Muslim Brotherhood. [Translation] "The claimant cannot be held responsible for the writings of a third person made in his absence... The panel does not distinguish between what his father was told and what was reported by the claimant in his claim for refugee protection, and the content of the complaints filed by the authorities against him." 2-The RPD wrongfully rejected the documents of the Egyptian authorities on the basis of a simple contradiction of the claimant's testimony. [Translation] "...the RPD did not have the expertise to assess the foreign documents" and ignored the presumption of truthfulness established in Maldonado.

The appellant is requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) [translation] "allow this appeal, set aside the RPD determination of the panel composed of Christian Fournier (sic), and grant the appellant the status of protected person; or set aside the RPD determination made by the panel composed of Christian Fournier (sic); and refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination."

The appellant is not requesting to present new evidence pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act2 (IRPA) and does not want a hearing to be held under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.
The Minister's representative did not intervene on appeal.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination, namely, that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.
The appeal is dismissed SCOPE OF THE APPEAL
In accordance with Huruglica,3 the RAD must apply the correctness standard of review to questions of fact, law and mixed fact and law.

I have conducted an independent analysis of all the evidence on the record, after listening carefully to the hearing, in order to form my own opinion concerning this refugee protection claim and to determine whether the RPD's determination is correct.
Having examined all of the testimonial and documentary evidence on the record, the RAD finds, as did the RPD, that the appellant is not credible.
The appellant believes that the RPD failed to properly assess his credibility, and that the impact on the decision is such that the appellant would not be persecuted in his country.
The very essence of this case is based on the appellant's credibility.

After listening to the recording, I conclude that the appellant's testimony was indirect and he did not answer the panel's questions. For example, the panel asked him for information about his roommate, who lived with the appellant after arriving from Egypt. Who made this request? The appellant answered that it was the person who helped him when he arrived in Canada. That person asked him to take him in. Did he know him previously? He was from the appellant's city. He was unable to identify the person who helped him at the mosque upon his arrival and who asked him in turn to help a fellow member of his faith community. The appellant told the panel that it was an individual. Another example is that the member asked the appellant if he had been accused of belonging to a group. The appellant answered that he was not a member of a group. He deflected the panel's rather simple questions several times and simply did not answer. This undermines his testimony and, therefore, his credibility.

With regard to the first item in the memorandum, which mentions that the Egyptian authorities questioned the appellant's father and the outcome of this matter, about his involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood, the appellant pointed out that at no time did the police tell his father that he was accused of being a member of that group. The RPD noted a contradiction between the testimony and the content of certain exhibits that the appellant submitted in support of his claim for refugee protection. What did he state in his testimony?

The appellant testified that the Egyptian authorities went to the family home on XXXX XXXX, 2018, took away the appellant's father and informed him that if the appellant returned to Egypt, he would be arrested. When told this, the appellant's father immediately informed his son, who filed a claim for protection.

The documents submitted4 are of the utmost importance to understanding this file. According to the appellant's testimony, he has no legal concerns other than the warrant. With respect to the content of the warrant, the panel asked the appellant whether he had been found guilty or accused of any activities prohibited by the Criminal Code. The answer was no. Had he been accused of being a member of a group? The answer again was no. Had he been sentenced or convicted? He answered yes, there was an arrest warrant. Finally, the panel asked him if the warrant mentioned a sentence. The answer was no. He added that he could be arrested at any time with the warrant.

The appellant was confronted with Exhibit P-2, where the Egyptian authorities accuse him of several things including disturbing the peace with a text prepared by the Muslim Brotherhood, participating in several protests with this group that has been banned by the authorities, and being responsible for the youth wing of the Muslim Brotherhood in a particular area. When asked to explain the contradictions between his previous testimony, which does not mention charges or indictments, and his own evidence, the appellant's reply was surprising. He stated: [translation] "they say that I am part of the Muslim Brotherhood. I am not a member, I am speaking about myself, I am not a member of any movement, it is my brother who is a member."

The member confronted him with his negative responses concerning all the evidence, even though it states in the warrant that he must serve a seven-year sentence. The appellant answered as follows: [translation] "it was issued in my absence...I misunderstood the question, I'm sorry...I don't know what would be said about me."

The RAD must reject the appellant's explanations about his own arrest warrant. His testimony is not consistent with his evidence, and he provided no explanation for the charges against him. According to the evidence he submitted, the Egyptian authorities consider the appellant to be a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, a group that is banned in several countries as it is considered to be a terrorist group that has committed many abuses against the civilian population and governments. The only thing he told the panel was that his brother was a member of this terrorist group. His testimony is clearly at odds with the evidence he submitted. It should be noted that the main, consequential and sensitive information in his evidence is not found in his written account in the BOC Form or in his testimony. He denied or minimized the information contained in his documents. This considerably undermines his credibility.
Consequently, the RAD finds that the RPD did not err.

The second element concerns the Egyptian authorities' documents, which according to the appellant were wrongly rejected. He adds that [translation] "the RPD does not have the expertise to assess foreign documents" and disregarded the presumption of truthfulness established by the jurisprudence. The RPD stated the following at paragraph 26 of its decision: [translation] "The panel grants no weight to the exhibits that he contradicted above, namely, the docket and the two reports by the authorities."

The RAD is of the opinion that the appellant's statement about the documents from Egypt shows that there is a misunderstanding. The appellant states that the panel does not have the expertise to assess the foreign documents whereas the RPD did not grant them any probative weight. Those are two different things. The RPD cannot state that a certain document is false or a forgery. It does not have the expertise to do so. Only an expert with their tools can analyze the paper, ink and typeset, among other things, and use their specialized knowledge to draw conclusions.

In this case, the RPD did not conclude that the Egyptian documents submitted were false or forgeries. On the contrary, the RPD did not weigh in on the materials or the medium on which the documents are printed or presented. After listening to and weighing the testimony and the appellant's explanations, the RPD stated that it did not assign any weight to the documents submitted. The RAD shares that opinion.
Consequently, the RAD finds that the RPD did not err.
For the reasons set out in this decision, the RAD finds that the RPD rendered the correct decision.

In light of all the facts cited above and after examining all the evidence, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of sections 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed (signed) Michel Jobin Michel Jobin September 1, 2020 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 SPR-1, Refugee Protection Division (RPD) record, Document 2: Basis of Claim Form - MB8-07192, pages 19 and 20. 2 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (S.C. 2001, c. 27). 3 Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v.
